title: Beyond the Binary: Duality, Non-Duality and the Semitic Third Space
subtitle: Why so many traditions say that two is not the last word: the One, the mirror of the pair, and the third space between.
summary: We see the world in pairs: light and dark, self and other. The contemplative traditions say duality is real but not ultimate. How Arabic grammar treats two as neither one nor many, three parables that see through surface opposites, the two ways of divine love, and practices for living rooted in the One.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an, Legge's Tao Te Ching).

title: Clean, Pure, and the Pork Question
subtitle: What the Bible means by clean, holy, dirty and impure, why the pig was forbidden, and the two Christian readings of whether the ban still stands.
summary: Clean is not the same as holy, and dirty is not the same as impure. The four words, the difference between ritual impurity and forbidden food, why the pig stood out, and the strongest case on each side of the Christian debate over eating pork.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. Scripture is quoted from the King James Version and Pickthall's Qur'an on this site. Both Christian positions are presented in their own terms; the site does not take a side.

title: On Truth, Part 1: What Is Truth?
subtitle: Worship's natural companion is truth. What the traditions mean by it, what holds it up, and what it costs.
summary: What do the scriptures and the philosophers mean by truth? Its pillars, why we are drawn to it, the parable of the painted well, how believers and non-believers see it, and what it asks of us.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own text, edited and fact-checked with AI. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an, Muller's Upanishads, Legge's Tao Te Ching).

title: On Truth, Part 2: The Crucible of Truth
subtitle: Transformation, technology and the universal thread: how to know you have found truth, and how to share it without building walls.
summary: The test of truth is the fruit it bears. How each tradition locates truth, a common thread without tribalism, truth in the age of AI, modern parables, science and theology as maps, and a further-study index.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own text, edited and fact-checked with AI. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an, Muller's Upanishads, Legge's Tao Te Ching, Besant's Bhagavad Gita, Johnston's Yoga Sutras).

title: On Truth, Part 3: Past Yes and No
subtitle: The collapse of the yes-or-no question, the self-sustaining loop, and the void of Genesis.
summary: Is every question a yes or a no? How Buddhist logic answers the question of a creator, the seed and the tree, the “without form, and void” of Genesis read as potential, four classical critiques, and Indra's net.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own text, edited and fact-checked with AI. It sets out a Buddhist line of thought in its own voice, beside the Bible; it is one tradition's view, not the site's verdict. Scripture is quoted from the King James Version on this site.

title: Promethean Shadows: Enoch 8 and the Arc of Human Progress
subtitle: The arts the fallen Watchers taught, read as a picture of human history: every leap in technique brings its own crisis of wisdom.
summary: In 1 Enoch 8 fallen angels teach humanity metalwork, cosmetics, herb-lore and star-lore, and the world is corrupted. Read as an allegory of human ages, from the forge to the algorithm, with parallels from Greece, Mesopotamia, Genesis and India.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. 1 Enoch is quoted from R. H. Charles's public-domain translation on this site, and Genesis from the King James Version. The Watcher-to-age mapping is the essay's interpretation, not the text's.

title: The Blind Sculptor and the Primordial Name
subtitle: On outside-in imitation, inside-out creation, and the gap between a machine's likeness and the image of God.
summary: A sculptor in a dark room carves a perfect horse without ever having seen one: the way machines learn. Adam looks at the animals and names them: the way the scriptures describe human knowing. What the difference means in an age of AI.
aiNote: From the Verses Across team's own essay, arranged into three lengths with AI and checked by the team. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an).

title: The Sanctity of Rhythm
subtitle: Enoch's astronomy, the numbers 3, 7 and 12, and reclaiming a living sense of time.
summary: We treat time as a commodity on a clock. The Astronomical Book of Enoch, the old base-12 and base-60 numbers, the patterns of 3, 7 and 12, music, and the evening-first day of Genesis all point to time as something living, and to ways of getting that rhythm back.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. 1 Enoch is quoted from R. H. Charles's public-domain translation on this site, and the Bible from the King James Version. The number symbolism is the essay's own reflection, not a scientific claim.

title: What If? The Untrodden Paths of Eden
subtitle: Three other ways the story of the two trees could have gone, and what each one shows about freedom, suffering and eternal life.
summary: Genesis tells of one choice: the fruit of knowledge, then exile. What if Adam and Eve had eaten only from the tree of life? Or from life first, then knowledge? Or knowledge first, and life afterward? Three thought experiments, with parables.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. The three scenarios, proverbs and parables are the essay's own imaginative reflections, not traditional texts. Scripture is quoted from the King James Version on this site.

title: If I Were the Devil
subtitle: A warning for our time. Inspired by Paul Harvey's 1965 radio broadcast "If I Were the Devil": a new piece written for today, not his words.
summary: How evil might quietly take a society apart, written as a mirror rather than a finger pointed at others, and then a way back.
aiNote: Drafted with AI from the Verses Across team's outline, in its own words, inspired by Paul Harvey's 1965 broadcast. Scripture is quoted from the King James Version on this site.

title: What Do You Worship?
subtitle: Everyone kneels somewhere. On the oldest question of the human heart, and how to tell what we really serve.
summary: Worship is not only what happens in a temple: it is where we give our attention, love and effort. How the traditions describe it, how it has changed through history, and one test that shows what any of us really serves.
aiNote: Drafted with AI from the Verses Across team's own outline, then edited and checked by the team. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an, Besant's Bhagavad Gita, Pusey's Augustine).
